newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ministers meet to prepare jobs summit.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers meet to prepare jobs summit.

text.p: European Union social affairs ministers met on Saturday in the small Luxembourg town of Echternach to prepare for a November jobs summit which will address the plight of the 15-nation bloc's unemployed.

"We have agreed to do everything possible," Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told a news conference after the informal meeting, adding that "what we don't want is a smoke-screen conference" which merely rehashed old ideas.
"There is a 16th member state -- 20 million unemployed (who) await legislative and administrative measures (on employment)."
Juncker, whose country took over the rotating EU presidency on July 1, has been careful to stress the proposed jobs summit can not produce "miracles".
He said Saturday's meeting had been about "taking stock of the reflections put to us".

Work already underway on employment issues would be speeded up and national reports on employment and examples of job schemes which worked well in member countries were due to be handed in by the end of July.
Juncker said it had also been agreed the so-called social partners - trade unions and employers - should be closely involved with the jobs summit.
Ministers, who arrived on Friday evening for the informal meeting, were due to continue their discussions over dinner and leave at midday on Sunday.

Earlier EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn told them that while expectations should not be raised that the summit alone would provide solutions for the unemployment problem in Europe, "it must be able to confirm a genuine commitment of member states in favour of employment."

Flynn said the "joint report on employment" being prepared for the summit would also look at the job creating potential of small and medium sized companies and initiatives of the European Investment Bank (EIB) in creating employment opportunities.
The EIB, the EU's lending arm, is being urged to step up its activities and help with more investment.
Employment was pushed to the top of the agenda at last month's EU summit in Amsterdam, when France agreed to an EU budget stability pact only in return for a resolution on jobs and growth.

The resolution reflected growing concern among Europe's citizens that in the austerity drive needed to get member states in shape for a single European currency, the EU was losing sight of social issues.
Flynn said he had four themes in mind to be addressed, namely the issues of employability, entrepreneurship focused on local employment initiatives, adaptability and equal opportunities.

Other questions on the table at the summit should include consultation of workers over company restructuring -- a problem highlighted recently by Renault's sudden announcement it was closing its profitable Vilvoorde plant in Belgium -- and the gap between available skills and those required by employers.
